nameStory: Silvery cinquefoil gets its shimmering name from the silvery-white undersides of its leaves, which catch the light like tiny mirrors when rustled by the wind. The word 'cinquefoil' comes from French meaning 'five leaves,' referring to the plant's distinctive five-leaflet arrangement that looks like an open hand.
description: Silvery cinquefoil is a low-growing perennial herb that forms spreading mats about 6-12 inches tall. Its most striking feature is the silvery-white, fuzzy undersides of its five-part leaves that contrast beautifully with the green tops. Small bright yellow flowers with five petals bloom throughout summer, looking like tiny wild roses. This European native has made itself at home in New England's disturbed soils and sunny spots.

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Five narrow leaflets arranged like fingers on a hand, dark green on top but strikingly silvery-white and fuzzy underneath - flip a leaf over to see the dramatic color difference

idTips.label: Flowers
idTips.description: Bright yellow flowers about half an inch across with five rounded petals and a small cluster of yellow stamens in the center, blooming in loose clusters

idTips.label: Growth Habit
idTips.description: Forms low, spreading mats with stems that can root where they touch the ground, rarely getting taller than your shin

idTips.label: Leaves
idTips.description: Leaflets have rolled-under edges and feel distinctly fuzzy to the touch, especially on the silvery undersides

habitat: Look for silvery cinquefoil in disturbed, well-drained soils like roadsides, old fields, gravel areas, and sandy spots. It thrives in full sun and poor soils where other plants struggle, often appearing along trails, in parking areas, and on dry slopes throughout New England.

seasonality.spring: New leaves emerge showing their characteristic silvery undersides, with the plant forming low green mats as stems begin spreading.
seasonality.summer: Peak blooming season with bright yellow flowers appearing from June through August, making identification easiest during this time.
seasonality.fall: Flowers fade and small dry seeds develop, while leaves may start to show wear but still retain their silvery undersides.
seasonality.winter: Dies back to ground level in harsh winters, though some leaves may persist in protected spots, appearing weathered but still showing traces of their silvery coating.

funFact: Despite being called 'silvery,' the plant doesn't actually contain any silver - the metallic shine comes from thousands of tiny white hairs that reflect light like a natural mirror, helping the plant stay cool in hot, sunny locations where it loves to grow.
confusionNotes: Other cinquefoils in New England lack the distinctive silvery-white leaf undersides - if you flip the leaf over and don't see that metallic shine, you're looking at a different species. Remember: silver underneath, silvery cinquefoil!
contextualKnowledge: As a member of the rose family, silvery cinquefoil is actually related to apples, strawberries, and roses, which explains why its five-petaled yellow flowers have that familiar rose-like appearance with their ring of stamens in the center.
compareHints: Among New England's cinquefoils, silvery cinquefoil is the only one with dramatically silver-white fuzzy leaf undersides - dwarf and common cinquefoil have plain green undersides, while rough cinquefoil has much larger, coarsely-toothed leaves. Sulphur cinquefoil is much taller and has pale yellow flowers instead of bright yellow ones.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Sulphur cinquefoil stands out from other New England cinquefoils primarily by its bright yellow flowers and consistently five-fingered leaves.
Among New England's cinquefoils, dwarf cinquefoil is distinguished by its truly prostrate, mat-forming habit with rooting runners.
Common cinquefoil differs from dwarf cinquefoil by its longer, more obvious runners and slightly larger flowers.
Unlike other cinquefoils in its genus which typically have five-part leaves (the name cinquefoil means 'five leaves'), mock strawberry has three-part leaves like true strawberries.
Unlike most other New England cinquefoils which have five leaflets, rough cinquefoil stands out with just three leaflets per leaf.
Lesser mock-strawberry differs from other cinquefoils by having three-part leaves instead of the typical five-part leaves (cinque means five in French).
Unlike its lowland cinquefoil relatives that spread by runners or grow as larger plants, dwarf mountain cinquefoil forms tiny, tight cushions and never leaves the alpine zone.

Among New England's cinquefoils, creeping cinquefoil is unique for its long trailing runners and five-leaflet leaves – most other cinquefoils like common cinquefoil and dwarf cinquefoil have three leaflets and don't spread by runners.

Intermediate cinquefoil differs from common New England cinquefoils like dwarf cinquefoil by its specific leaflet count and arrangement, and from sulphur cinquefoil by its smaller stature and different leaf texture.
Unlike its inland cinquefoil relatives, coast cinquefoil has adapted specifically to maritime conditions with its more compact, mat-forming growth and thicker, more succulent-like leaves.
